Section: 1. General Principles
ECG is used clinically to detect and assess cardiac chamber hypertrophy.
The principal ECG changes associated with ventricular hypertrophy include increased QRS amplitude and
duration, changes in QRS vectors, ST-segment and T-wave abnormalities, and P-wave abnormalities.
ECG criteria for hypertrophy have historically been compared with clinical, autopsy, echocardiographic,
CT, and magnetic resonance assessments of ventricular mass.
ECG remains clinically useful because it is widely available, convenient, and inexpensive.
No ECG criterion should be interpreted as an absolute measurement of anatomic chamber mass.

Section: 2. Left Ventricular Hypertrophy — LVH
Most commonly used ECG criteria for LVH are based on QRS voltage.
The Sokolow–Lyon criterion uses the sum of S-wave amplitude in V1 and R-wave amplitude in V5 or V6. A
value of 35 mm is a commonly cited threshold in the source.
The Cornell voltage criterion uses the sum of S-wave amplitude in V3 and R-wave amplitude in aVL. The
source lists thresholds of 28 mm in men and 20 mm in women.
Other voltage criteria include R in aVL ≥11 mm, R in aVF ≥20 mm, and S in V1 ≥23 mm.
QRS duration may be increased in LVH. This can appear as diffuse QRS prolongation or increased time
from QRS onset to the R-wave peak in V5 or V6.
Voltage-duration products and other composite criteria have also been developed.

Section: 3. LVH Diagnostic Performance
Different LVH criteria do not identify exactly the same patients.
Sensitivity of individual ECG criteria for LVH is generally low, often below 50%, while specificity is
generally high, often around 85–90%.
Diagnostic performance varies with the criterion and the patient population.
Interpretations should specify which criteria were used.
Automated ECG systems should consider multiple validated criteria rather than relying on a single
voltage measurement.
AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 ECG Hypertrophy — RAG Source Page 1
QRS voltage can be influenced by age, sex, body habitus, and population characteristics.

Section: 4. Right Ventricular Hypertrophy — RVH
RVH may produce increased R-wave amplitude in right precordial leads, increased S-wave amplitude in
left precordial leads, rightward QRS axis, and other QRS changes.
The source lists a commonly cited criterion of R in V1 + S in V5 or V6 ≥10.5 mm.
An R-wave peak in V1 with QRS duration ≥0.12 seconds and a QR pattern in V1 are among described
criteria or supporting findings.
Supporting findings can include an RSR pattern in V1 with QRS duration ≥0.12 seconds, rightward axis
patterns, and T-wave abnormalities in right precordial leads.
No single criterion or limited set of criteria should be used exclusively for RVH diagnosis.
RVH probability should be interpreted in light of clinical diagnoses such as congenital heart disease,
valvular disease, or chronic pulmonary disease.
RVH criteria should be considered in relation to age, sex, body habitus, and other patient characteristics.

Section: 5. Biventricular Hypertrophy
ECG detection of biventricular hypertrophy has particularly low sensitivity because increased QRS
vectors from RVH and LVH can partially cancel each other.
Biventricular hypertrophy should be suggested when accepted criteria for both RVH and LVH are present.
Right axis deviation in a patient with ECG evidence of LVH, prominent S waves in V5 or V6, tall biphasic
R/S complexes, and signs of right atrial abnormality can support suspicion of biventricular hypertrophy.
Because sensitivity is low, absence of ECG criteria does not exclude biventricular hypertrophy.

Section: 6. Left Atrial Abnormality
Abnormal P-wave patterns can be associated with left or right atrial abnormalities.
A total P-wave duration of 120 ms or more is commonly present in patients with ECG signs considered to
represent left atrial abnormality.
A purely negative P wave in V1 can be suggestive but is not specific by itself.
Left atrial abnormality is associated with changes in the later P-wave forces and may be accompanied by
P-wave axis changes.

Section: 7. Right Atrial Abnormality
Right atrial abnormality is typically associated with increased P-wave amplitude and a tendency toward
rightward P-wave vector shift.
A tall upright P wave in lead II greater than 2.5 mm is a characteristic finding.
Prominent initial positivity of the P wave in V1 or V2 of 1.5 mm or more also indicates right atrial
abnormality.
Rightward P-wave axis and a peaked P-wave form can provide supporting evidence.
Total P-wave duration is usually normal in right atrial abnormality, although important exceptions occur
in some patients with repaired congenital heart disease.

Section: 8. Pediatric Considerations
Pediatric ECG voltage criteria for ventricular hypertrophy are age-dependent.
AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009 ECG Hypertrophy — RAG Source Page 2
The source provides separate age-related criteria for pediatric LVH and RVH.
Adult voltage thresholds should not be automatically applied to children.
When pediatric criteria are used, age and the appropriate pediatric reference values must be retained as
metadata.

Section: 9. Clinical Interpretation Rules
ECG findings associated with chamber hypertrophy should be interpreted together rather than as
isolated abnormalities.
A positive voltage criterion does not by itself establish anatomic hypertrophy.
A negative ECG does not reliably exclude hypertrophy because ECG sensitivity is limited.
The clinical context and, when needed, imaging should be considered when confirming chamber
hypertrophy.
Criteria may behave differently across patient populations and body habitus.

Section: 10. RAG Retrieval Rules
Use one ECG concept per chunk.
Keep each voltage formula and its threshold in the same chunk.
Never separate a threshold from the lead configuration to which it applies.
Keep adult and pediatric criteria in separate chunks.
Keep LVH, RVH, biventricular hypertrophy, left atrial abnormality, and right atrial abnormality separate.
Preserve limitations such as low sensitivity and population dependence because they prevent
overconfident retrieval-based answers.
Do not ingest the paper's reference list or author/contributor disclosures as clinical knowledge.
Recommended metadata: source_id=AHA_ECG_HYPERTROPHY_2009; topic; chamber; criterion_type;
age_group; keywords; original page if available.

Section: 2021 ESC Heart Failure — RAG Knowledge
Source
English • Text only • No tables • Retrieval-oriented condensed source
Source identity. McDonagh TA, Metra M, Adamo M, et al. 2021 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and
treatment of acute and chronic heart failure. European Society of Cardiology / European Heart Journal,
2021.
Purpose. This document is a clean, condensed representation of clinically useful facts from the ESC
guideline. It is designed for retrieval and question answering. References, long evidence discussions,
repeated prose, and unrelated material are excluded.
RAG note. Each section below contains short, self-contained facts. Numerical thresholds remain attached
to their clinical context.

Section: 1. Heart Failure Definition
Heart failure (HF) is a clinical syndrome associated with symptoms and signs caused by a structural
and/or functional cardiac abnormality.
Symptoms and signs alone are not sufficient to establish the diagnosis. Objective evidence of cardiac
structural or functional abnormality is required.
Common symptoms include breathlessness, fatigue, and ankle swelling.
Possible signs include elevated jugular venous pressure, pulmonary crackles, and peripheral edema.

Section: 2. Heart Failure Phenotypes
HFrEF: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. LVEF is ≤40%.
HFmrEF: heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction. LVEF is 41–49%. Symptoms and/or signs of
HF are present; raised natriuretic peptides and/or relevant structural abnormalities support the
diagnosis.
HFpEF: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. LVEF is ≥50%, with symptoms and signs plus
objective evidence of relevant structural or functional abnormalities and/or raised natriuretic peptides.
LVEF means left ventricular ejection fraction and is commonly assessed by echocardiography.

Section: 3. Chronic Heart Failure Diagnosis
When HF is suspected, assess symptoms and/or signs, risk factors, previous cardiovascular disease, and
the ECG.
An abnormal ECG increases the likelihood of HF. A normal ECG makes HF less likely.
In the non-acute diagnostic pathway, NT-proBNP ≥125 pg/mL or BNP ≥35 pg/mL prompts further
evaluation.
Echocardiography is used to assess cardiac structure and function and to measure LVEF.
After objective abnormalities are identified, define the HF phenotype as HFrEF, HFmrEF, or HFpEF.
The underlying etiology should then be investigated because it can influence management.

Section: 4. NYHA Functional Classification
NYHA Class I: no limitation of physical activity. Ordinary physical activity does not cause undue
symptoms.
ESC 2021 Heart Failure — RAG Source Page 1
NYHA Class II: slight limitation of physical activity. The patient is comfortable at rest, but ordinary
physical activity causes symptoms.
NYHA Class III: marked limitation of physical activity. The patient is comfortable at rest, but activity less
than ordinary causes symptoms.
NYHA Class IV: unable to carry out physical activity without discomfort. Symptoms may be present at
rest and increase with activity.

Section: 5. Major Heart Failure Etiologies
Important causes and etiologies to investigate include:
• Coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction.
• Hypertension.
• Valvular heart disease.
• Arrhythmias.
• Dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive, and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathies.
• Congenital heart disease.
• Myocarditis and selected infectious causes.
• Peripartum cardiomyopathy.
• Takotsubo syndrome.
• Relevant toxins or cardiotoxic exposures.

Section: 6. Diagnostic Tests
ECG: identifies electrical and structural clues. A normal ECG makes HF less likely.
BNP / NT-proBNP: natriuretic peptides used in the HF diagnostic pathway.
Echocardiography: assesses cardiac structure and function and measures LVEF.
Coronary assessment: coronary angiography, CT coronary angiography, or stress imaging may be used
when CAD is suspected.
Ambulatory ECG: may be used when an arrhythmia is suspected.
Cardiac magnetic resonance: can characterize cardiomyopathies, myocarditis, and other structural
abnormalities.
Laboratory tests: selected tests help identify contributing conditions and complications.

Section: 7. Acute Heart Failure
Acute heart failure (AHF) is a separate diagnostic and management pathway from chronic/non-acute HF.
For suspected AHF, rule-out thresholds are BNP <100 pg/mL, NT-proBNP <300 pg/mL, or MR-proANP
<120 pg/mL.
For NT-proBNP, age-specific rule-in values include >450 pg/mL for age <55 years, >900 pg/mL for age
55–75 years, and >1800 pg/mL for age >75 years.
Initial laboratory assessment may include troponin, serum creatinine, electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen or
urea, TSH, and liver function tests.
D-dimer is considered when acute pulmonary embolism is suspected. Procalcitonin may be considered
when infection or pneumonia is suspected. Arterial blood gas analysis is used when respiratory distress
requires precise oxygen and carbon dioxide assessment. Lactate and pH are relevant when cardiogenic
shock or hypoperfusion is suspected.
ESC 2021 Heart Failure — RAG Source Page 2
Comprehensive echocardiography is part of the evaluation after AHF is confirmed or strongly suspected.

Section: 8. Acute Pulmonary Edema
Acute pulmonary edema is related to lung congestion.
Clinical features can include dyspnea with orthopnea, respiratory failure with hypoxaemia or
hypercapnia, tachypnea above 25 breaths/min, and increased work of breathing.
When indicated, treatment may include oxygen or non-invasive respiratory support, intravenous
diuretics, and intravenous vasodilators when systolic blood pressure is sufficiently high.
If acute pulmonary edema is associated with low cardiac output in advanced HF, inotropes, vasopressors,
and/or mechanical circulatory support may be required.

Section: 9. Treatment — Core Retrieval Facts
HFrEF: major guideline-directed drug classes include ACE inhibitors or ARNI, beta-blockers,
mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and SGLT2 inhibitors. Diuretics are used to relieve congestion
when fluid retention is present.
HFmrEF: diuretics are recommended when congestion is present. Other treatments may be considered
according to the clinical context.
HFpEF: management focuses on identifying and treating underlying causes, cardiovascular risk factors,
and comorbidities, with treatment of congestion when present.
Treatment choices depend on the individual clinical situation, contraindications, renal function, blood
pressure, and comorbidities. Detailed dosing is intentionally omitted from this RAG source.

Section: 10. Advanced Heart Failure
Advanced HF requires all specified criteria to be present despite optimal medical treatment.
Severe and persistent symptoms are defined as NYHA class III or IV.
Severe cardiac dysfunction may include LVEF ≤30%, isolated right ventricular failure, non-operable
severe valve abnormalities, non-operable severe congenital abnormalities, or persistently
high/increasing BNP or NT-proBNP together with severe LV diastolic dysfunction or structural
abnormalities consistent with HFpEF.
Severe recurrent events include pulmonary or systemic congestion requiring high-dose intravenous
diuretics, low-output episodes requiring inotropes or vasoactive drugs, or malignant arrhythmias causing
more than one unplanned visit or hospitalization in the previous 12 months.
Severely impaired exercise capacity includes inability to exercise, a 6-minute walk test distance <300 m,
peak VO₂ <12 mL/kg/min, or peak VO₂ <50% of predicted when the limitation is considered cardiac in
origin.

Section: 11. RAG Retrieval Rules
Use one main clinical idea per chunk.
Keep numerical thresholds together with the condition they describe, especially when acute and
non-acute thresholds differ.
Keep abbreviations explicit: HF, HFrEF, HFmrEF, HFpEF, LVEF, BNP, NT-proBNP, NYHA, AHF.
Separate diagnosis, phenotype classification, etiology, treatment, acute HF, and advanced HF into
different chunks.
Do not ingest reference lists, author lists, page headers, URLs, or repeated guideline boilerplate as
clinical knowledge.
ESC 2021 Heart Failure — RAG Source Page 3
Recommended metadata: source_id=ESC_HF_2021; topic; section; keywords; original page if available.

Section: 1. What is an ECG?
An ECG (electrocardiogram) records the electrical activity of the heart
over time. Each heartbeat produces a repeating pattern of waves. The
ECG captures and traces this activity as a continuous curve.

Section: 1.1 How Are Signals Recorded?
Electrodes are placed on the skin (arms, legs, chest). Each pair of
electrodes forms a lead that captures the signal from a different angle.
• A standard ECG has 12 leads.
• 12 points of view on the same heart, at the same time.

Section: 1.2 Sampling Frequency
Sampling frequency is the number of measurements of the electrical
signal taken per second.
• Higher frequency → more temporal detail.
• Higher frequency → heavier data (larger file size).
ECG at 500 Hz: 500 measurements per second. Each of the 12 leads
independently records the heart's electrical voltage 500 times in 1
second, all at the same time points.

Section: 1.3 Data Dimensions (Standard ECG)
Item Value
Sampling frequency 500 Hz
Typical recording duration 10 seconds
Points per lead 500 × 10 = 5,000 points
Number of leads 12
Total values per patient 5,000 × 12 = 60,000 values

Section: 2. How to Read an ECG
Every heartbeat follows a consistent sequence of electrical waves:
P → QRS → T
• In a healthy person, this cycle lasts about 0.6–1.0 seconds.
• The order and timing of these waves are identical across all 12
ECG leads.
• What changes from lead to lead is the appearance, shape, size,
and direction.
• Each lead captures the same electrical event from a different
angle.

Section: 2.1 The Waves
P Wave
• Represents: Atrial contraction (upper chambers push blood into
ventricles).
• Normal duration: ~80–120 ms
• Abnormal if: Absent → atrial problem (e.g., atrial fibrillation)
QRS Complex
• Represents: Ventricular contraction, the actual heartbeat. Most
visible peak.
• Normal duration: ~80–100 ms
• Abnormal if: Wide and deformed → bundle branch block or
ventricular arrhythmia
T Wave
• Represents: Ventricular repolarization (ventricles recharge
electrically).
• Abnormal if: Inverted or flattened → sign of ischemia (lack of
oxygen to the heart)

Section: 2.2 The Intervals
RR Interval
• Definition: Distance between two consecutive R peaks
• Gives: Heart rate
• Abnormal if: Irregular → arrhythmia
PR Interval
• Definition: From the start of P to the start of QRS
• Measures: Atrial → ventricular conduction time
• Abnormal if: Too long → AV block
ST Segment
• Definition: The line between the end of QRS and the start of T
• Should be: On the baseline (isoelectric)
• Abnormal if: Elevated or depressed → possible myocardial
infarction (heart attack)
QT Interval
• Definition: From the start of QRS to the end of T
• Abnormal if: Too long → risk of serious arrhythmia (e.g., Torsade
de Pointes)

Section: 3.1 Atrial Fibrillation (AF)
A heart rhythm disorder where the atria no longer contract in an
organized way: irregularity detection in beat sequences.
• ECG pattern: Absent P waves + irregularly irregular RR intervals
• Clinical note: Most common arrhythmia

Section: 3.2 ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)
A myocardial infarction (heart attack) with ST segment elevation.
• ECG pattern: ST elevation ≥1 mm in ≥2 contiguous leads +
reciprocal depression
Note: Elevation = the signal goes ABOVE the line. Depression = the
signal goes BELOW the line. When both are seen simultaneously,
elevation in some leads and depression in others, this confirms a real MI
from two angles. The location of elevation and depression follows a
precise anatomical logic.
The heart has 4 walls. Each wall is "watched" by specific leads:

Section: 3.3 Bundle Branch Blocks (LBBB / RBBB)
A bundle branch block is a delay or interruption in the electrical
conduction through the ventricles. The electrical impulse originates in
the atria, passes through the AV node, then propagates rapidly into the
ventricles via two branches (right and left).
• ECG pattern: Wide QRS >120 ms + specific lead patterns:
RBBB (Right Bundle Branch Block) → typical RSR' pattern
○
in lead V1 (two peaks)
LBBB (Left Bundle Branch Block) → typical wide QS
○

• Classification type: Morphology classification

Section: 3.4 Left Ventricular Hypertrophy (LVH)
Increase in the muscle mass of the left ventricle. The left ventricle must
sometimes work harder (e.g., in hypertension or valvular stenosis). To
compensate, its muscle thickens → it becomes more massive.
Result on ECG: R waves are much taller (greater amplitude), as a larger
muscle generates a stronger electrical signal.
• ECG pattern: High-voltage R waves
• Sokolow-Lyon criterion: SV1 + RV5 ≥ 35 mm → LVH
• Modified Cornell criterion: R wave in aVL > 1.2 mV → LVH
• Classification type: Voltage measurement task

Section: 1. What is an MRI?
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a non-invasive medical imaging
technique that uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves to create
detailed images of the organs and tissues inside the body.

Section: 1.1 How Are MRIs Recorded?
The body is mostly water. Water contains hydrogen atoms. MRI uses a
strong magnet to align those atoms, then fires radio waves to disturb
them. As the atoms "snap back" to alignment, they emit a signal. A
computer turns that signal into an image.

Section: 1.2 Why MRI for the heart specifically?
MRI is the gold standard for cardiac imaging because it can show:
• Heart movement: MRI films the heart beating in real time →
Function
• Scar tissue (fibrosis): Dead heart muscle from a past heart
attack shows up as a bright white patch → Tissue damage
• Chamber size & wall thickness: Precise measurements of the
ventricles → Structure
• Blood flow (perfusion): Contrast agent injected → shows which
areas receive enough blood → Blood supply

Section: 2. Cardiac MRI Sequences
A "sequence" is a different type of MRI scan. Unlike ECG which always
records the same signal, MRI has multiple "modes" called sequences.
Each sequence highlights different tissue properties.

Section: 2.1 Cine MRI
A video of the beating heart, typically 20–30 frames per cardiac cycle.
Shows how well the walls move and contract. Used to measure ejection

Section: 2.2 LGE (Late Gadolinium Enhancement)
A contrast agent (Gadolinium) is injected. Dead/scarred tissue holds the
agent longer → appears bright white. The gold standard for detecting old
heart attacks.

Section: 4.1 Functional Abnormalities (from Cine MRI)
• Heart failure (reduced EF): The ventricle isn't pumping out
enough blood per beat. HFrEF (reduced ejection fraction) directly
detectable via EF; HFpEF (preserved EF) needs volumes/filling
pattern.
• Wall motion abnormalities: Segments can be hypokinetic
(weakly), akinetic (not at all), or dyskinetic (wrong direction). Sign
of localized damage.
• Dyssynchrony: One wall contracts late relative to others →
mechanically inefficient pump.

Section: 4.2 Structural Abnormalities (from Cine MRI + Short Axis Stack)
• Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM): Ventricle chamber enlarged/
stretched out, walls thin. Usually accompanied by low EF.
• Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM): Walls abnormally thick,
chamber normal or small. Often genetic. Dangerous due to
obstruction and sudden cardiac events.
header: 4.2 Structural Abnormalities (from Cine MRI + Short Axis Stack)

text:
Section: 4.3 Tissue/Scar Abnormalities (from LGE)
• Prior myocardial infarction: LGE shows subendocardial (inner
layer only) vs transmural (full wall thickness) patterns. Location
matches coronary artery blocked.
• Sudden death risk (via LGE extent %): More scar tissue (% of
total heart muscle) → higher risk of dangerous arrhythmias and
sudden cardiac death.

Section: 4.4 Inflammatory / Infiltrative Disease (from T1/T2 Mapping)
• Myocarditis (acute inflammation): Elevated T2 (edema/
inflammation) and sometimes elevated T1.
• Edema: Excess fluid in tissue. Marker of acute injury or
inflammation. Elevated T2 is the key signal.
• Amyloidosis / infiltrative disease
• Iron overload (hemochromatosis)
• Diffuse fibrosis (via ECV)
